claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical correlation analysis results with correlation coefficients, confidence intervals, and p-values.

claims.claim: The mean target knee joint angles for the fixed-end reference contractions were 28.2±2.3°, 68.1±10.1°, and 83.6±7.9° for the short, long, and very long muscle lengths, respectively.
claims.source: The mean target knee joint angles determined from the optical motion analysis system for the fixed-end reference contractions were 28.2±2.3°, 68.1±10.1°, and 83.6±7.9° for the short, long, and very long muscle lengths, respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by kinematic measurements presented in the Results section.

claims.claim: The mean target knee joint angles for the stretch-hold contractions were 28.2±4.3°, 68.7±18.4°, and 86.1±19.2° for the short, long, and very long muscle lengths, respectively.
claims.source: For the stretch-hold contractions, the mean target knee joint angles were 28.2±4.3°, 68.7±18.4°, and 86.1±19.2° for the short, long, and very long muscle lengths, respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by kinematic measurements presented in the Results section.

claims.claim: During the stretch-hold contractions, the measured knee joint rotations during the amplitude-matched dynamometer-imposed rotations were 9.0±4.3°, 14.7±2.3°, and 15.7±2.8° to the short, long, and very long muscle lengths, respectively.
claims.source: During the stretch-hold contractions, the measured knee joint rotations during the amplitude-matched dynamometer-imposed rotations were 9.0±4.3°, 14.7±2.3°, and 15.7±2.8° to the short, long, and very long muscle lengths, respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by kinematic measurements presented in the Results section.

claims.claim: The programmed dynamometer rotations were 14.8±0.4°, 15.4±0.4°, and 15.2±0.3° for the short, long, and very long muscle lengths, respectively.
claims.source: The respective programmed dynamometer rotations were 14.8±0.4°, 15.4±0.4°, and 15.2±0.3°.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by dynamometer programming data presented in the Results section.

claims.claim: This is the first in vivo experiment that has attempted to estimate rFE at more than two muscle lengths.
claims.source: To our knowledge, this is the first in vivo experiment that has attempted to estimate rFE at more than two muscle lengths, and the first to use shear-wave tensiometry.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the existing literature and represents a novel aspect of their study.

claims.claim: This is the first in vivo experiment to use shear-wave tensiometry to estimate rFE.
claims.source: To our knowledge, this is the first in vivo experiment that has attempted to estimate rFE at more than two muscle lengths, and the first to use shear-wave tensiometry.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the existing literature and represents a novel methodological aspect of their study.

claims.claim: Corrected knee extension torques were significantly higher during the steady-state phase of the stretch-hold compared with the fixed-end reference contractions at both the long and very long muscle lengths.
claims.source: We found that corrected knee extension torques were significantly higher during the steady-state phase of the stretch-hold compared with the fixed-end reference contractions at both the long and very long muscle lengths, whereas squared PT shear-wave speeds were significantly higher only at the very long muscle length.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing torques between contraction conditions at different muscle lengths.

claims.claim: Squared PT shear-wave speeds were significantly higher during the steady-state phase of the stretch-hold compared with the fixed-end reference contractions only at the very long muscle length.
claims.source: We found that corrected knee extension torques were significantly higher during the steady-state phase of the stretch-hold compared with the fixed-end reference contractions at both the long and very long muscle lengths, whereas squared PT shear-wave speeds were significantly higher only at the very long muscle length.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing squared shear-wave speeds between contraction conditions at different muscle lengths.

claims.claim: The greatest rFE was found at the very long muscle length for both rFETQ and rFEWS measures.
claims.source: For both rFETQ and rFEWS measures, we found the greatest rFE at the very long muscle length.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the highest rFE values at the very long muscle length.

claims.claim: In vivo rFE is maximised during submaximal voluntary contractions of the human quadriceps at a very long muscle length.
claims.source: Taken together, rFETQ and rFEWS findings indicate that in vivo rFE is maximised during submaximal voluntary contractions of the human quadriceps at a very long muscle length, and that in vivo rFE is more strongly correlated with VL muscle fascicle length than fascicle stretch amplitude.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing greatest rFE at very long muscle length.

claims.claim: In vivo rFE is more strongly correlated with VL muscle fascicle length than fascicle stretch amplitude.
claims.source: Taken together, rFETQ and rFEWS findings indicate that in vivo rFE is maximised during submaximal voluntary contractions of the human quadriceps at a very long muscle length, and that in vivo rFE is more strongly correlated with VL muscle fascicle length than fascicle stretch amplitude.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the correlation analysis showing significant relationships with fascicle length but not stretch amplitude.

claims.claim: The findings are in accordance with a previous study by Bakenecker et al., 2020 that found significant rFE only at a long (10.7±5.5%), but not at a short (1.3±3.1%) muscle length.
claims.source: This is in accordance with a previous study with a similar setup, where we also found significant rFE only at a long (10.7±5.5%), but not at a short (1.3±3.1%) muscle length (Bakenecker et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with cited previous work by Bakenecker et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Similar findings have been reported by Shim and Garner, 2012 at short (no rFE) and long (4.7%) quadriceps' muscle lengths.
claims.source: Similar findings have been reported by Shim and Garner, 2012 at short (no rFE) and long (4.7%) quadriceps' muscle lengths.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Shim and Garner, 2012, which reported similar findings.

claims.claim: Power et al., 2013 tested at 60° knee flexion for their short muscle length condition, which would result in a longer muscle length and therefore significant rFE based on the current study's data.
claims.source: Unlike the aforementioned studies, which either tested at a common knee flexion angle of 40° knee flexion or confirmed that the short muscle length was situated on the ascending limb of the quadriceps' torque-angle relationship, Power et al., 2013 tested at 60° knee flexion for their short muscle length condition, which would result in a longer muscle length and therefore significant rFE based on our data (Figures 1 and 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing the current study's findings with the methodology of Power et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Bullimore et al., 2007 showed that rFE increases with increasing stretch amplitude until a critical amplitude (9 mm of stretch) when the stretch ends on the descending limb of the force-length relationship.
claims.source: For example, Bullimore et al., 2007 showed that rFE increases with increasing stretch amplitude until a critical amplitude (9 mm of stretch) when the stretch ends on the descending limb of the force-length relationship.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bullimore et al., 2007, which demonstrated this relationship.

claims.claim: Hisey et al., 2009 showed that rFE only increases with increasing stretch amplitude until a critical amplitude (12 mm of stretch) when the stretch ends at very long muscle fascicle lengths on the descending limb of the force-length relationship.
claims.source: Hisey et al., 2009 later showed that rFE only increases with increasing stretch amplitude until a critical amplitude (12 mm of stretch) when the stretch ends at very long muscle fascicle lengths on the descending limb of the force-length relationship (i.e. 9 mm longer than the optimum length).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hisey et al., 2009, which demonstrated this relationship.

claims.claim: It is unlikely that greater stretch amplitudes contributed to greater rFE at the long and very long muscle lengths compared with the short muscle length.
claims.source: As we observed no significant repeated-measures linear relationship between VL fascicle stretch amplitude and rFETQ (Figure 2), it is unlikely that greater stretch amplitudes contributed to greater rFE at the long and very long muscle lengths compared with the short muscle length.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the lack of significant correlation between stretch amplitude and rFE.

claims.claim: Based on the findings of Hisey et al., 2009, it is unlikely that greater stretch amplitudes to the short muscle length would have changed the rFE values observed.
claims.source: Based on the findings of Hisey et al., 2009, where increasing stretch amplitude did not increase the amount of rFE at a target muscle length 3 mm shorter than the muscle's optimal length for maximum isometric force production, it is further unlikely that greater stretch amplitudes to the short muscle length (i.e. on the ascending limb of the force-length relationship) would have changed the rFE values we observed.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the findings of Hisey et al., 2009 applied to the current study's context.

claims.claim: The increase in rFE with muscle length could potentially be due to a greater increase in stiffness of a passive elastic structure, such as titin, as it is stretched to longer lengths.
claims.source: The increase in rFE with muscle length could potentially be due to a greater increase in stiffness of a passive elastic structure, such as titin (Rassier and Herzog, 2005), as it is stretched to longer lengths.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative and based on a proposed mechanism cited from Rassier and Herzog, 2005.

claims.claim: rFE magnitudes based on corrected knee extension torques of 2±5%, 7±5%, and 12±8% at the short, long, and very long muscle lengths are in accordance with findings from Seiberl et al., 2012.
claims.source: In this study, we found rFE magnitudes based on corrected knee extension torques of 2±5%, 7±5%, and 12±8% at the short, long, and very long muscle lengths, respectively. Based on PT shear-wave-speed measures, we observed rFE magnitudes of 8±12%, 6±10%, and 38±27% at the same respective lengths. Except for the rFEWS values at the very long muscle length, the rFE values from this study are in accordance with findings from the study of Seiberl et al., 2012, which also had participants perform submaximal voluntary stretch-hold and fixed-end reference contractions of the human quadriceps.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with cited work by Seiberl et al., 2012.

claims.claim: At a similar crank-arm angle (100° knee flexion) compared with the very long muscle length condition (104±6°), Seiberl et al., 2012 observed rFE magnitudes of 7–11% and 3–5% at 30% and 60% of the maximum voluntary activity level, respectively.
claims.source: At a similar crank-arm angle (100° knee flexion) compared with what we used for the very long muscle length condition (104±6°), Seiberl et al., 2012 observed rFE magnitudes of 7–11% and 3–5% at 30% and 60% of the maximum voluntary activity level, respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Seiberl et al., 2012, which reported these rFE magnitudes.

claims.claim: Other studies that investigated the human plantar flexors and the adductor pollicis showed similar rFE magnitudes (7–13%) during submaximal voluntary stretch-hold contractions.
claims.source: Other studies that investigated the human plantar flexors and the adductor pollicis showed similar rFE magnitudes (7–13%) during submaximal voluntary stretch-hold contractions (Oskouei and Herzog, 2006; Oskouei and Herzog, 2005; Pinniger and Cresswell, 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Oskouei and Herzog, 2006, Oskouei and Herzog, 2005, and Pinniger and Cresswell, 2007.

claims.claim: rFE magnitudes greater than ~15% have only been found for electrically stimulated human muscles.
claims.source: rFE magnitudes greater than ~15% have only been found for electrically stimulated human muscles (Cook and McDonagh, 1995).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Cook and McDonagh, 1995.

claims.claim: The rFEWS values above 25% calculated in this study might be erroneous.
claims.source: The rFEWS values above 25% (see Figure 1B) we calculated might therefore be erroneous, which is supported by the much lower than expected normalised squared PT shear-wave speeds determined during the fixed-end reference contractions at the very long muscle length (see Figures 3 and 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the unexpectedly high rFEWS values and comparison with literature values.

claims.claim: The average agreement between normalised squared PT shear-wave speeds and estimated PT forces was 62% at the very long muscle length compared with 86% and 91% at the short and long muscle lengths, respectively.
claims.source: Unsurprisingly, the average agreement between normalised squared PT shear-wave speeds and estimated PT forces was worst at this muscle length at 62% compared with 86% and 91% at the short and long muscle lengths, respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing shear-wave speeds and estimated forces.

claims.claim: The accuracy of the shear-wave-speed estimates, or PT force estimates, might decrease as the PT's orientation changes relative to the tibia's long axis.
claims.source: This might be because the accuracy of the shear-wave-speed estimates, or PT force estimates, decreases as the PT's orientation changes relative to the tibia's long axis (Draganich et al., 1987), however this deserves further research.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative and based on a cited mechanism from Draganich et al., 1987.

claims.claim: Obtaining plausible shear-wave speeds from the PT proved to be very difficult.
claims.source: In general, obtaining plausible shear-wave speeds from the PT proved to be very difficult.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the experimental experience described in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: Martin et al., 2018 could not calculate shear-wave speeds from the PT during parts of the gait cycle.
claims.source: In some of our participants (n=5), the shear-wave tensiometry technique resulted in unusable data, which is not that surprising, considering that Martin et al., 2018 also could not calculate shear-wave speeds from the PT during parts of the gait cycle (see their Supplementary Figure 6).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2018, which reported similar difficulties.

claims.claim: An average agreement between squared PT shear-wave speeds and estimated PT forces above 90% was found for only four participants.
claims.source: For the remaining participants in the current study whose shear-wave speeds could be quantified, the accuracy of the measurements across different knee joint angles is questionable considering that we found an average agreement between squared PT shear-wave speeds and estimated PT forces above 90% for four participants only (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: PT shear-wave-speed measurements became implausible during passive conditions where the MTU was at rest, during active conditions with stretch under high tension, and during maximal voluntary contractions.
claims.source: PT shear-wave-speed measurements also became implausible during passive conditions where the MTU was at rest, during active conditions with stretch under high tension (Figure 4B), and during maximal voluntary contractions.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the Discussion and shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Squared shear-wave speeds changed drastically across different joint angles, despite similar torque levels.
claims.source: Further, squared shear-wave speeds changed drastically across different joint angles, despite similar torque levels (Figure 4B/E and C/F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B/E and C/F.

claims.claim: Quantifying PT loads can be problematic with shear-wave tensiometry and the PT shear-wave speeds estimated by this technique might be inaccurate.
claims.source: Taken together, this indicates that quantifying PT loads can be problematic with shear-wave tensiometry and that the PT shear-wave speeds estimated by this technique might be inaccurate.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the various problems observed with shear-wave tensiometry measurements.

claims.claim: The main assumption of shear-wave tensiometry is that the shear-wave propagation speed depends primarily on tendon axial stress under physiological loads.
claims.source: The main assumption of shear-wave tensiometry is that the shear-wave propagation speed depends primarily on tendon axial stress under physiological loads (Martin et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2018, which established this assumption.

claims.claim: This assumption might not hold true under very low or high physiological loads.
claims.source: Even if this assumption holds true, which might not be the case under very low or high physiological loads (Blank et al., 2022; Sarvazyan et al., 2013), axial stress is influenced by both the force in the tendon and the tendon's architecture (i.e. the width and thickness of the tendon).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blank et al., 2022 and Sarvazyan et al., 2013, which suggest limitations to the assumption.

claims.claim: Axial stress is influenced by both the force in the tendon and the tendon's architecture.
claims.source: Even if this assumption holds true, which might not be the case under very low or high physiological loads (Blank et al., 2022; Sarvazyan et al., 2013), axial stress is influenced by both the force in the tendon and the tendon's architecture (i.e. the width and thickness of the tendon).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the relationship between stress, force, and cross-sectional area.

claims.claim: Martin et al., 2020 suggests that the calibration gain required to estimate tendon stress based on tendon shear-wave speed appears to increase with increasing tendon aspect ratios.
claims.source: A recent study by Martin et al., 2020 suggests that the calibration gain required to estimate tendon stress based on tendon shear-wave speed appears to increase with increasing tendon aspect ratios (i.e. increasing tendon width relative to tendon thickness).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2020, which reported this relationship.

claims.claim: When the tendon's architecture changes under different contraction conditions, shear-wave speeds could vary at the same tendon stress.
claims.source: Accordingly, when the tendon's architecture changes (e.g. through deformation of the tendon due to an applied stress) (Kuervers et al., 2021) under different contraction conditions (e.g. during a stretch-hold contraction that covers different joint angles and contraction intensities), shear-wave speeds could vary at the same tendon stress.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the relationship between tendon architecture and shear-wave speed, with citation to Kuervers et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Shear-wave speeds may not accurately reflect tendon stress unless the changes in tendon architecture are accounted for.
claims.source: Thus, shear-wave speeds may not accurately reflect tendon stress unless the changes in tendon architecture are accounted for.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the discussion about tendon architecture changes affecting shear-wave speeds.

claims.claim: In former studies, high correlations between squared shear-wave speed and torque measures were found when muscle activities and corresponding tendon stresses were low during preferred-speed walking.
claims.source: In former studies (Keuler et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2018), high correlations between squared shear-wave speed (≤80 m2 s–2) and torque measures (≤200 Nm) were found when muscle activities and corresponding tendon stresses were low during preferred-speed walking (≤50 MPa).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Keuler et al., 2019 and Martin et al., 2018, which reported these correlations.

claims.claim: Under higher knee extension torques and presumably higher tendon stresses at submaximal muscle activity levels, the estimated PT force-angle relationships were not reflected by the squared shear-wave-speed measures.
claims.source: In contrast, under the higher knee extension torques (112–296 Nm) and presumably higher tendon stresses (>50 MPa) at the submaximal muscle activity levels that were used in this study, the estimated PT force-angle relationships were not reflected by the squared shear-wave-speed measures (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Squared shear-wave-speed estimates were unreasonably high when participants increased their activation level during the maximal voluntary contractions.
claims.source: Additionally, squared shear-wave-speed estimates were unreasonably high when participants increased their activation level during the maximal voluntary contractions in the first part of the experiment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: High tendon stresses and changing tendon dimensions might be problematic for accurately estimating PT tendon loads based on shear-wave-speed measures.
claims.source: Therefore, high tendon stresses and changing tendon dimensions might be problematic for accurately estimating PT tendon loads based on shear-wave-speed measures.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed problems with shear-wave speed measurements at high loads.

claims.claim: Estimates of PT shear-wave speeds might be affected by differences in subcutaneous tissue thickness between individuals.
claims.source: Estimates of PT shear-wave speeds might additionally be affected by differences in subcutaneous tissue thickness between individuals as Martin et al., 2018 showed that the propagating shear wave within the deep tendon was not identical to the shear wave propagating along the skin.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative and based on a cited observation from Martin et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Compared with the Achilles tendon, the PT has more overlying subcutaneous tissue and is smaller in thickness in its mid-region.
claims.source: Compared with the Achilles tendon, the PT has more overlying subcutaneous tissue (Bravo-Sánchez et al., 2019) and is smaller in thickness in its mid-region (Coombes et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bravo-Sánchez et al., 2019 and Coombes et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Thicker subcutaneous tissue over a thinner tendon might result in poorer shear-wave propagation within the PT compared with the Achilles tendon and less accurate shear-wave-speed estimates.
claims.source: These factors might result in poorer shear-wave propagation within the PT compared with the Achilles tendon and less accurate shear-wave-speed estimates.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from anatomical differences between tendons.

claims.claim: Previous in vivo experiments that examined rFE during voluntary contractions have identified a number of participants not showing rFE, called non-responders.
claims.source: Previous in vivo experiments that examined rFE during voluntary contractions have identified a number of participants not showing rFE (Hahn et al., 2012; Hahn et al., 2007; Oskouei and Herzog, 2006; Tilp et al., 2009). These participants were subsequently called non-responders.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hahn et al., 2012, Hahn et al., 2007, Oskouei and Herzog, 2006, and Tilp et al., 2009.

claims.claim: There was no participant in the current study's dataset who consistently showed no rFE across the three muscle lengths tested.
claims.source: However, in opposition to the idea of there being a true non-responder, there was no participant in our dataset who consistently showed no rFE across the three muscle lengths we tested.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the current study.

claims.claim: There is no true non-responder to rFE.
claims.source: We thus speculate there is no true non-responder.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative and based on the observation that no participant consistently showed no rFE.

claims.claim: Paternoster et al., 2021 showed that voluntary rFE appeared inconsistently in the same participants across five testing sessions, whereas during submaximal tetanic electrical muscle stimulation, all participants consistently showed rFE.
claims.source: This speculation is supported by recent work by Paternoster et al., 2021, who showed that voluntary rFE appeared inconsistently in the same participants across five testing sessions, whereas during submaximal tetanic electrical muscle stimulation, all participants consistently showed rFE.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Paternoster et al., 2021, which reported these findings.

claims.claim: Having participants match muscle activity levels through voluntary effort, rather than through artificial stimulation, likely adds variability to rFE estimates and might contribute to the 'non-responder' phenomenon.
claims.source: Indeed, having participants match muscle activity levels through voluntary effort, rather than through artificial stimulation, likely adds variability to rFE estimates (especially over a short duration analysis window like the one used here), and might contribute to the 'non-responder' phenomenon.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison between voluntary and electrically stimulated contractions.

claims.claim: rFE values could be influenced by different preloads prior to the stretch phase of the stretch-hold contractions at the short, long, and very long muscle lengths.
claims.source: Although we performed feedback-controlled contractions based on EMG recordings to ensure the same level of superficial quadriceps' activity during stretch-hold and fixed-end reference contractions and we assessed VL muscle fascicle stretch magnitudes, our rFE values could be influenced by different preloads prior to the stretch phase of the stretch-hold contractions at the short, long, and very long muscle lengths.
claims.evidence: The claim acknowledges a potential limitation of the study based on the experimental design.

claims.claim: Using a preload prior to a stretch-hold contraction at the MTU level results in shortening-isometric-stretch-isometric muscle fascicle behavior, where the initial shortening of muscle fascicles increases with an increasing preload or a shorter initial muscle length.
claims.source: Due to the relatively high compliance of human lower limb MTUs, using a preload prior to a stretch-hold contraction at the MTU level results in shortening-isometric-stretch-isometric muscle fascicle behavior, where the initial shortening of muscle fascicles increases with an increasing preload or a shorter initial muscle length.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about the behavior of compliant MTUs during contractions.

claims.claim: rFE can be influenced by the amount of shortening preceding stretch.
claims.source: As rFE can be influenced by the amount of shortening preceding stretch (Lee et al., 2001) and active shortening can induce residual force depression (i.e. a reduction in the steady-state force following shortening Abbott and Aubert, 1952; Granzier et al., 1989), differences in muscle fascicle shortening across the three tested muscle lengths could have influenced the estimated rFE magnitudes.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2001, Abbott and Aubert, 1952, and Granzier et al., 1989.

claims.claim: Active shortening can induce residual force depression.
claims.source: As rFE can be influenced by the amount of shortening preceding stretch (Lee et al., 2001) and active shortening can induce residual force depression (i.e. a reduction in the steady-state force following shortening Abbott and Aubert, 1952; Granzier et al., 1989), differences in muscle fascicle shortening across the three tested muscle lengths could have influenced the estimated rFE magnitudes.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Abbott and Aubert, 1952 and Granzier et al., 1989.

claims.claim: Differences in muscle fascicle shortening across the three tested muscle lengths could have influenced the estimated rFE magnitudes.
claims.source: As rFE can be influenced by the amount of shortening preceding stretch (Lee et al., 2001) and active shortening can induce residual force depression (i.e. a reduction in the steady-state force following shortening Abbott and Aubert, 1952; Granzier et al., 1989), differences in muscle fascicle shortening across the three tested muscle lengths could have influenced the estimated rFE magnitudes.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the cited literature about shortening effects on force.

claims.claim: Stretch amplitudes and muscle fascicle lengths were assessed from only a limited region within the VL muscle.
claims.source: Further, we only assessed stretch amplitudes and muscle fascicle lengths from a limited region within the VL muscle and we needed to perform linear extrapolation to estimate fascicle lengths, so we recommend that future studies investigate a muscle with shorter and less curved fascicles to better evaluate the influence of stretch amplitude and fascicle length on rFE.
claims.evidence: The claim acknowledges a limitation of the study's methodology.

claims.claim: Linear extrapolation was needed to estimate fascicle lengths.
claims.source: Further, we only assessed stretch amplitudes and muscle fascicle lengths from a limited region within the VL muscle and we needed to perform linear extrapolation to estimate fascicle lengths, so we recommend that future studies investigate a muscle with shorter and less curved fascicles to better evaluate the influence of stretch amplitude and fascicle length on rFE.
claims.evidence: The claim acknowledges a methodological limitation of the study.

claims.claim: Future studies should investigate a muscle with shorter and less curved fascicles to better evaluate the influence of stretch amplitude and fascicle length on rFE.
claims.source: Further, we only assessed stretch amplitudes and muscle fascicle lengths from a limited region within the VL muscle and we needed to perform linear extrapolation to estimate fascicle lengths, so we recommend that future studies investigate a muscle with shorter and less curved fascicles to better evaluate the influence of stretch amplitude and fascicle length on rFE.
claims.evidence: The claim is a recommendation based on the limitations identified in the current study.

claims.claim: Assessing PT loads with shear-wave tensiometry might be inaccurate based on the low agreement (<90%) across tested muscle lengths between normalised squared PT shear-wave speeds and normalised PT forces estimated from corrected knee extension torques.
claims.source: Additionally, the low agreement (<90%) across tested muscle lengths between normalised squared PT shear-wave speeds and normalised PT forces estimated from corrected knee extension torques suggests that assessing PT loads with shear-wave tensiometry might be inaccurate.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing poor agreement between the two measurement methods.

claims.claim: Sixteen healthy males participated in the study initially.
claims.source: Sixteen healthy males (age 27.9±5.3 years; height 186.3±5.6 cm; weight 83.4±8.6 kg) gave free written informed consent prior to participating in the study, 11 of whom (age 28.4±5.9 years; height 187.1±5.8 cm; weight 82.8±8.0 kg) had data that could be analysed as their PT shear-wave speeds could be calculated.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by participant demographic data presented in the Materials and methods section.

claims.claim: Eleven participants had data that could be analysed as their PT shear-wave speeds could be calculated.
claims.source: Sixteen healthy males (age 27.9±5.3 years; height 186.3±5.6 cm; weight 83.4±8.6 kg) gave free written informed consent prior to participating in the study, 11 of whom (age 28.4±5.9 years; height 187.1±5.8 cm; weight 82.8±8.0 kg) had data that could be analysed as their PT shear-wave speeds could be calculated.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by participant data presented in the Materials and methods section.

claims.claim: The recruited participants were relatively tall to increase the chances of successfully securing the tendon tapper device over a longer PT.
claims.source: The recruited participants were relatively tall to increase the chances of successfully securing the tendon tapper device over a longer PT.
claims.evidence: The claim explains the rationale for the participant selection criteria.

claims.claim: Pilot testing revealed that individuals should be at least 181 cm tall for the study.
claims.source: As pilot testing revealed that individuals should be at least 181 cm, we tested males only because we were not able to recruit any female participants that were this tall.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on pilot testing data that informed the study design.

claims.claim: Only males were tested because no female participants could be recruited that were at least 181 cm tall.
claims.source: As pilot testing revealed that individuals should be at least 181 cm, we tested males only because we were not able to recruit any female participants that were this tall.
claims.evidence: The claim explains the rationale for testing only male participants.

claims.claim: All participants were free of knee injuries and neuromuscular disorders.
claims.source: All participants were free of knee injuries and neuromuscular disorders.
claims.evidence: The claim describes the inclusion criteria for participants.

claims.claim: All experimental procedures were approved by the local Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Sport Science at Ruhr University Bochum and conformed with the Declaration of Helsinki.
claims.source: All experimental procedures were approved by the local Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Sport Science at Ruhr University Bochum and conformed with the Declaration of Helsinki.
claims.evidence: The claim describes the ethical approval for the study.

results.result: Residual force enhancement based on corrected knee extension torques (rFETQ) was significant at long (7±5%) and very long (12±8%) muscle lengths, but not at short (2±5%) muscle lengths. Statistical analysis revealed significant main effects of contraction condition and muscle length, with a significant interaction between these factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C27-C33, and C53 provide converging evidence from torque measurements, statistical analyses (ANOVA with F-statistics and p-values), and post hoc comparisons showing muscle length-dependent rFE. The experimental design with EMG-matched contractions (C24-C25) controls for activation differences, strengthening the conclusion that muscle length affects rFE.

results.result: Residual force enhancement based on squared patellar tendon shear-wave speeds (rFEWS) was significant only at the very long muscle length (38±27%), but not at short (8±12%) or long (6±10%) muscle lengths. Statistical analysis showed significant main effects and interactions similar to torque-based measures.
results.evaluation: While claims C15 and C34-C40 provide statistical evidence for rFEWS at very long muscle length, the validity is questionable given: (1) high variability (±27%), (2) acknowledged measurement difficulties (C21, C73-C78), (3) poor agreement with estimated PT forces at very long length (C71: 62% vs 86-91% at other lengths), and (4) authors' own concerns about accuracy (C70, C78, C105). The measurement technique's reliability is insufficiently established.

results.result: Significant positive correlations were found between VL fascicle length and both rFETQ (r=0.63, p=0.001) and rFEWS (r=0.52, p=0.017), indicating that in vivo rFE is more strongly correlated with muscle fascicle length than stretch amplitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C16 and C46 provide statistical correlation data with appropriate repeated-measures analysis, confidence intervals, and significant p-values. This is further supported by the lack of significant correlations with stretch amplitude (C17, C45), providing a clear contrast. The conclusion (C56-C57) is well-supported by the correlation data and consistent with in vitro findings cited (C4, C61-C62).

results.result: No significant relationships were found between VL fascicle stretch amplitude and rFETQ (r=0.33, p=0.126) or rFEWS (r=0.29, p=0.201), despite significant differences in stretch amplitude across muscle lengths (short: 3.7±2.1 mm, long: 6.0±1.8 mm, very long: 6.3±2.8 mm).
results.evaluation: Claims C17, C41-C45, and C63 provide consistent evidence that stretch amplitude varied significantly across conditions (ANOVA: F=9.10, p=0.002) but did not correlate with rFE. The statistical analysis is appropriate with correlation coefficients, confidence intervals, and p-values. However, the study acknowledges limitations in fascicle tracking (C102-C103) that could affect measurement accuracy.

results.result: Squared PT shear-wave-speed-angle relationships did not agree with estimated PT force-angle relationships, with average agreement of only 62% at very long muscle length compared to 86% and 91% at short and long lengths. Only 4 of 11 participants showed >90% agreement across all muscle lengths.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C19, C71, C75, C78, and C105 provide converging evidence from multiple analyses showing poor agreement between shear-wave measurements and force estimates. The quantitative agreement metrics (62% vs 86-91%) and participant-level data (4/11 with >90% agreement) support the conclusion. This is further substantiated by methodological concerns (C73-C77, C79-C91) and comparison with prior literature (C85-C87).

results.result: The study concludes that increasing muscle length rather than stretch amplitude contributes more to rFE during submaximal voluntary contractions of the human quadriceps, with greatest rFE observed at very long muscle length.
results.evaluation: Claims C20 and C55-C57 represent the main conclusion, which is well-supported by: (1) significant rFE at long and very long but not short lengths (C14-C15), (2) significant correlations with fascicle length but not stretch amplitude (C16-C17, C46, C45), and (3) consistency with in vitro literature (C4, C61-C62). The conclusion logically follows from the experimental data despite concerns about shear-wave tensiometry accuracy.

results.result: Multiple technical and methodological issues were identified with shear-wave tensiometry for measuring PT loads, including: (1) 5/16 participants excluded due to unusable data, (2) implausible measurements during passive conditions and maximal contractions, (3) drastic changes in shear-wave speeds despite similar torque levels, (4) potential effects of tendon architecture changes, subcutaneous tissue thickness, and high tendon stresses on measurement accuracy.
results.evaluation: Claims C21, C73-C91 provide extensive documentation of technical problems with shear-wave tensiometry through: (1) participant exclusion data (C21: 5/16), (2) experimental observations (C73, C76-C77), (3) comparison with prior literature showing similar difficulties (C74, C85-C87), and (4) theoretical considerations about measurement assumptions (C79-C84, C89-C91). The authors appropriately acknowledge these limitations and provide mechanistic explanations supported by citations.

results.result: EMG-matched contractions successfully maintained similar muscle activity levels between stretch-hold and fixed-end reference contractions across all muscle lengths, with differences within the allowed 6% variation and no significant differences in post hoc comparisons.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C26 demonstrate successful experimental control of muscle activation through: (1) significant main effect of contraction condition (F=12.59, p=0.005) but (2) non-significant post hoc comparisons at all muscle lengths (p>0.05) with differences within the pre-specified 6% tolerance. Biceps femoris activity was also low and similar (C26: 4.6% vs 5.0%), indicating minimal antagonist co-contraction. This validates the experimental design for isolating rFE effects.

results.result: Kinematic measurements confirmed target knee joint angles were achieved for fixed-end (28.2±2.3°, 68.1±10.1°, 83.6±7.9°) and stretch-hold contractions (28.2±4.3°, 68.7±18.4°, 86.1±19.2°) at short, long, and very long muscle lengths. Measured knee joint rotations during stretch-hold contractions (9.0±4.3°, 14.7±2.3°, 15.7±2.8°) were close to programmed dynamometer rotations (~15°).
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 provide kinematic validation data showing: (1) target angles were achieved with reasonable precision, (2) actual knee joint rotations were close to programmed values at long and very long lengths, though lower at short length (9.0° vs 14.8°). The discrepancy at short length could affect interpretation but is acknowledged. The use of motion capture to correct for axis misalignment strengthens the torque measurements.

results.result: This study represents the first in vivo experiment to estimate rFE at more than two muscle lengths and the first to use shear-wave tensiometry for this purpose.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 assert novelty based on the authors' literature knowledge. While these claims cannot be independently verified without comprehensive literature review, they are plausible given: (1) the experimental design testing three muscle lengths, (2) the novel application of shear-wave tensiometry to rFE measurement, and (3) citations to prior work testing only two muscle lengths (C8-C9, C58-C59). The novelty claims are appropriately qualified with 'to our knowledge.'

results.result: The current findings are consistent with previous in vivo studies showing muscle length-dependent rFE in human quadriceps and other muscles, with rFE magnitudes (2-12% for torque-based measures) falling within the typical range for voluntary contractions (7-13%).
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 and C66-C69 appropriately contextualize the current findings within prior literature, showing consistency with Bakenecker et al. 2020 (C58), Shim and Garner 2012 (C59), and explaining discrepancies with Power et al. 2013 (C60) based on methodological differences. The rFE magnitudes are appropriately compared to literature values (C66-C69), with the caveat that rFEWS values >25% are likely erroneous (C70).

results.result: The lack of relationship between stretch amplitude and rFE is consistent with in situ findings showing that rFE increases with stretch amplitude only until a critical amplitude on the descending limb of the force-length relationship, and that stretch amplitude does not increase rFE at shorter muscle lengths.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 appropriately interpret the current findings (C63) in light of in situ literature (C61-C62 citing Bullimore et al. 2007 and Hisey et al. 2009). The inference that greater stretch amplitudes at short length would not change rFE (C64) is reasonable based on cited evidence. The proposed mechanism involving titin stiffness (C65) is appropriately speculative and cited.

results.result: The study found no consistent 'non-responders' to rFE across the three muscle lengths tested, suggesting that the non-responder phenomenon may be due to variability in voluntary muscle activation rather than true absence of rFE.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C96 address the non-responder phenomenon through: (1) observation that no participant consistently showed no rFE across all conditions (C93), (2) support from Paternoster et al. 2021 showing inconsistent voluntary rFE but consistent electrically-stimulated rFE (C95), and (3) logical inference about voluntary activation variability (C96). However, the conclusion is somewhat speculative (C94) and limited by the short analysis window and submaximal contractions used.

results.result: The study acknowledges that rFE values could be influenced by different preloads prior to stretch at different muscle lengths, which could cause varying amounts of fascicle shortening that affect rFE through residual force depression.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C101 appropriately acknowledge a limitation of the experimental design. The concern is well-founded based on: (1) known MTU compliance effects (C98), (2) cited evidence that shortening affects rFE (C99: Lee et al. 2001) and causes force depression (C100: Abbott and Aubert 1952, Granzier et al. 1989), and (3) logical inference about potential confounding (C101). This represents good scientific practice in acknowledging limitations.

results.result: The study acknowledges limitations in fascicle length measurements, including assessment from only a limited VL region and need for linear extrapolation, recommending future studies investigate muscles with shorter and less curved fascicles.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C104 appropriately acknowledge methodological limitations in fascicle tracking. The limitations are realistic given: (1) VL has long, curved fascicles that extend beyond the ultrasound field of view, (2) linear extrapolation introduces uncertainty, and (3) the recommendation for future work (C104) is reasonable. These limitations do not invalidate the main findings but appropriately qualify the fascicle length measurements.

results.result: The study recruited 16 healthy males (age 27.9±5.3 years, height 186.3±5.6 cm), of whom 11 had analyzable data. Participants were selected to be tall (≥181 cm) to accommodate the shear-wave tensiometry device, which limited recruitment to males only.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C112 provide clear participant demographics and selection rationale. The exclusion of 5/16 participants (C21, C107) due to technical issues is concerning but honestly reported. The height-based selection (C108-C109) and resulting male-only sample (C110) is a limitation for generalizability but is transparently explained. Ethical approval is documented (C112).

results.result: At the long muscle length, four outliers were detected in squared PT shear-wave-speed data (two from stretch-hold, two from fixed-end conditions) using a 4 MAD criterion, resulting in reduced sample size (n=9) for this condition.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C23 document outlier detection and exclusion using an appropriate statistical method (4 MAD criterion, cited to Leys et al. 2013). The specific outlier values are reported transparently. However, the high rate of outliers (4/22 measurements = 18%) at the long muscle length specifically raises concerns about measurement reliability at this condition, consistent with broader concerns about shear-wave tensiometry accuracy.

results.result: The introduction provides background on residual force enhancement (rFE) as a history-dependent muscle property, its observation across structural scales, independence from stretch velocity, dependence on muscle length, relationship with stretch amplitude, and introduces shear-wave tensiometry as a measurement technique.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C13 provide appropriate background context through citations to established literature. The claims accurately represent prior work on: rFE definition (C1: Cook and McDonagh 1995, Edman et al. 1978), multi-scale observations (C2), velocity independence (C3), length dependence (C4), stretch amplitude effects (C5-C6), in vivo findings (C7-C9), and shear-wave tensiometry validation (C10-C13). These provide necessary context for the current study.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that rFEWS values above 25% are likely erroneous and that high tendon stresses, changing tendon dimensions, and anatomical factors (subcutaneous tissue thickness, tendon geometry) may compromise shear-wave tensiometry accuracy for PT measurements.
results.evaluation: Claims C70, C72, C88, and C91 represent appropriate self-critical evaluation of the shear-wave tensiometry results. The acknowledgment that rFEWS values >25% are likely erroneous (C70) is supported by comparison with literature (C69) and poor agreement data (C71). The proposed explanations (C72, C88, C91) are speculative but reasonable and appropriately qualified. This demonstrates scientific integrity in acknowledging measurement limitations.
